sections.overview: The red junglefowl is a wild galliform bird of the pheasant family, native to South and Southeast Asia and the principal wild ancestor of the domestic chicken. Whole-genome comparisons support an early contribution from the Southeast Asian subspecies Gallus gallus spadiceus, followed by gene flow among chicken populations and other junglefowl; domestication was not a simple, isolated event. Some regional chicken genomes also carry introgressed DNA from grey junglefowl (Gallus sonneratii), with lesser or rarer signals from Ceylon junglefowl (Gallus lafayettii) and green junglefowl (Gallus varius); these findings do not displace red junglefowl as the main ancestor.
sections.identification: Males reach 65–78 cm in total length and 672–1,450 g; females are smaller at 41–46 cm and 485–1,050 g. These ranges include marked sexual size dimorphism and are Cornell Lab’s reference measurements. The wild adult male has a bright red comb and wattles, orange-gold neck feathers, a dark iridescent body, and long curved feathers over the tail. Females are smaller-looking and mottled brown, with a short tail and camouflage suited to nesting on the ground. A study of the Thai subspecies Gallus gallus spadiceus found breeding males with long golden neck hackles, unlike the shorter black feathers outside the breeding period. A wild-type outline alone cannot establish genetic purity, because domestic ancestry may be invisible in appearance. Domestic chickens have also been selected for rapid growth, so breed size and body form are not reliable norms for wild birds.
sections.habitat: Its native range spans the Indian subcontinent and much of mainland and island Southeast Asia, with regional subspecies occupying different areas. It uses old and secondary forest, mangroves, and forest edges, often feeding in a clearing or plantation beside cover.
sections.diet: This opportunistic omnivore takes seeds, fruits, and small invertebrates, including ants, beetles, and termites; the mix changes with local and seasonal availability. It scratches through soil and leaf litter with its feet before pecking at food, often visiting open ground in the early morning and evening. Its digestive tract includes a crop and muscular gizzard; the gizzard mechanically breaks down ingested food.
sections.behavior: Wary and mostly terrestrial, red junglefowl can fly strongly when alarmed and commonly roost in trees at night. Field observations describe small, changing groups: a male may accompany one or several females, while solitary males and females are also seen. Males crow repeatedly, often before dawn, and crowing helps reveal their presence; calls and displays also communicate between birds, though social patterns vary with place and season.
sections.reproduction: Breeding schedules differ by region: a two-year study of the subspecies Gallus gallus spadiceus in Malaysian agricultural landscapes recorded nests year-round, with a local peak in December. Nests averaged about four eggs, and captive incubation lasted roughly 19.5 days, close to three weeks. In Hainan, field researchers observed only females tending the brood, while accounts from southern Yunnan report both sexes incubating eggs; parental roles vary among the populations studied. Chicks hatch covered in down and leave the nest soon; a natural-history account places full feathering at about four to five weeks and sexual maturity near five months, somewhat later in females.
sections.ecology: Field observations and local reports from Thailand and Malaysia identify wild cats and birds of prey among predators of adult junglefowl. In Hainan, nest monitoring found predation to be a major cause of breeding failure, with coucals and rodents recorded at experimental nests and reptiles proposed as other potential predators.
sections.conservation: BirdLife International’s global IUCN assessment published in 2024 classifies the species as Least Concern, a global risk category that does not guarantee the security of each local population. An Indian Wildlife Institute of India project reported a fragmented distribution and growing pressures in several states, and found ten domestic-chicken hybrids among 220 birds sampled at captive centres. A 2023 genome comparison found domestic ancestry of about 20–50 percent in the modern wild populations sampled, relative to museum birds collected roughly a century earlier, with strong variation among individuals and places; habitat change and contact with free-ranging poultry remain local concerns.
